vision.description: Set the direction before you design the solution
vision.whatIsIt: Vision for Change sets out why $projectName matters, how it will improve patient care and staff experience and what good looks like in everyday clinical and administrative work.
vision.userInsight: $projectName landed best when it was framed as a clinical workflow and behaviour change, not a technology rollout
vision.whyThisMatters:
Reduces confusion about what $projectName is (and isn't) and protects trust in the change early.
 Prevents the programme being judged only on technology rather than the intended workflow improvement.
 Provides a consistent narrative across clinical, operational and admin audiences, reducing rumour-driven resistance.
vision.quickRealityCheck:
Can staff describe $projectName in one sentence? Does it reflect real pressures, not just programme goals?
 Are leaders saying the same thing consistently? Do people understand what will change in their day-to-day work?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CLEAR AND COMPELLING
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Vision is simple, inspiring and focused on patient care, staff experience and better ways of working.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: UNDERSTOOD AND SHARED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Staff at all levels can explain in their own words why $projectName matters and what will change..

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CONSISTENTLY COMMUNICATED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Leaders reinforce the vision regularly and use it to guide decisions and priorities.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: GROUNDED IN REAL SITUATIONS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Vision reflects the day-to-day challenges teams face and the improvements $projectName will bring.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: GUIDES ACTIONS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Vision helps teams make choices, solve problems and stay focused on what matters

risksIfYouDont.title: SEEN AS A TECHNOLOGY ROLLOUT
risksIfYouDont.body: Focus stays on the tool rather than the workflow and behaviour change.

risksIfYouDont.title: CONFUSION AND MIXED MESSAGES
risksIfYouDont.body: Different teams hear different things, leading to uncertainty about the reason $projectName is being introduced.

risksIfYouDont.title: LOW ENGAGEMENT AND RESISTANCE
risksIfYouDont.body: Staff don't see the relevance to their day-to-day work and are less likely to adopt $projectName.

risksIfYouDont.title: INCONSISTENT ADOPTION
risksIfYouDont.body: Without a shared vision, use will vary widely across teams and services.

risksIfYouDont.title: BENEFITS NOT REALISED
risksIfYouDont.body: Without a clear direction, efforts drift and the value of $projectName is not achieved

case_for_change.description: $projectName must solve a problem that staff clearly recognise
case_for_change.whatIsIt: A Case for Change explains the real clinical and operational pressures $projectName is responding to, why change is needed now and why current  Ways of working are becoming unsustainable.
case_for_change.userInsight: $projectName was most effective when it clearly addressed real operational pressures such as backlogs, wait times and admin burdens.
case_for_change.whyThisMatters: Prevents confusion over whether $projectName is about productivity, wellbeing, backlog reduction or system replacement. Helps teams agree on the workflow changes needed to realise the benefits. Reduces early resistance by focusing on the problem that needs solving, not the novelty of $projectName.
case_for_change.quickRealityCheck: Can we explain why change is needed now? Are the benefits specific and measurable? Can leaders explain the change in one simple story? Is the problem clearly defined or are you starting with $projectName as the answer?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: $projectName NOT SEEN AS A TECHNICAL ROLLOUT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: $projectName is consistently understood as a clinical workflow and behaviour change, not a technology rollout

whatGoodLooksLike.title: LOWER COGNITIVE LOAD
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Clinicians experience lower cognitive load, better patient interaction and stronger day-to-day usability

whatGoodLooksLike.title: RESISTANCE REDUCTION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Reduces early resistance by focusing on the problem that needs solving, not the novelty of $projectName

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CLEAR PROBLEM STATEMENT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The problem $projectName is solving is specific, evidence-based and easy to explain.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: COMPELLING REASON TO ACT NOW
whatGoodLooksLike.body: There is urgency, not just a general desire to improve.

risksIfYouDont.title: STALLED ADOPTION
risksIfYouDont.body: Adoption stalls once the novelty fades because the purpose was never clear.

risksIfYouDont.title: DISENGAGEMENT
risksIfYouDont.body: Productivity narratives trigger suspicion and disengagement in $projectNames introduction.

risksIfYouDont.title: SCALING JUSTIFICATION STRUGGLES
risksIfYouDont.body: Leaders struggle to justify scaling because there is no credible “why now” and “what problem”

risksIfYouDont.title: BUSINESS OUTCOMES NOT LINKED
risksIfYouDont.body: Business Outcomes are not clearly linked to $projectName

risksIfYouDont.title: DISAGREEMENTS REGARDING THE PROBLEM
risksIfYouDont.body: Stakeholders do not agree on the problem statement.

sponsorship.description: Make $projectName clinically led and operationally owned, not IT driven
sponsorship.whatIsIt: Sponsorship means visible clinical and operational senior leaders driving $projectName as service improvement, supporting teams, removing barriers and building confidence to support adoption. Governance provides the structure for making clear timely decisions, so $projectName is introduced safely, consistently and at scale by having the right clinical, digital and safety checks in place.
sponsorship.userInsight: $projectName succeeded when strong clinical and operational sponsorship ensured $projectName was delivered as a clinical service improvement, not an IT led change, with leaders driving adoption, behaviours and redesign. Clear proportionate governance enabled safe timely decisions and supported $projectName scaling across clinical, operational and digital teams.
sponsorship.whyThisMatters:
Visible senior clinical and operational leadership builds trust, reduces resistance and enables pace and scale.
 Ensures $projectName is a clinical workflow change with clinical direction and operational ownership of local redesign.
 Sponsors remove barriers, support teams and make the decisions related to risk and workflow needed to embed change.
 Drives timely and clear decisions through defined decision making, governance cadence and active oversight.
 Enables safe, compliant use by ensuring assurance (IG, DPIA, Cyber, clinical safety and consent) is in place before clinical deployment.
 Supports scaling beyond pilots by managing risks transparently and creating a controlled organisation wide approach.
sponsorship.quickRealityCheck:
Are senior leaders actively showing support? Do sponsors demonstrate behaviours they expect from others?
 Are sponsors listening to feedback and responding? Are sponsors using the same consistent story?
 Are roles clear across business, tech, legal, risk and Ops? Who actually owns the decision, risk and sign off?
 Is there a clear escalation path when something fails? Are policies being followed in practice, not just documented?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CLEAR SPONSORSHIP IN PLACE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Clear credible sponsorship in place – named SRO, clinical sponsor (e.g. Medical Director/CCIO) and operational lead with ownership beyond digital/IT.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: VISIBLE LEADERSHIP
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Visible leadership driving change on the ground – actively engaging teams, reinforcing new behaviours and removing barriers to adoption.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: OPERATIONAL OWNERSHIP
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Operational ownership embedded early and leading workflow redesign.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: FRONTLINE FEEDBACK
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Frontline feedback is heard and acted on.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CLEAR GOVERNANCE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: There is a clear $projectName governance forum aligned to existing clinical and operational structures, with clear decision rights, escalation routes and documented approval authority.

risksIfYouDont.title: FAILURE TO SCALE
risksIfYouDont.body: Without senior clinical and operational leadership, adoption depends on individual enthusiasts and fails to scale across services.

risksIfYouDont.title: NO HUMAN IN THE LOOP
risksIfYouDont.body: Workflow issues and new ways of working, including "Human in the Loop" review and approval, may not be owned or resolved.

risksIfYouDont.title: SLOW UPTAKE
risksIfYouDont.body: Without visible senior backing, teams are less confident to change practice, delaying adoption and limiting impact.

risksIfYouDont.title: DELAYED DECISION MAKING
risksIfYouDont.body: Decisions are delayed because ownership is unclear.

risksIfYouDont.title: NO GOVERNANCE
risksIfYouDont.body: Without governance, there is no clear decision making between IG, IT and clinical/operational teams, which may lead to delays, hidden risk and pilots that never transition into controlled organisation wide roll outs.

change_network.description: Use trusted peers as champions to drive adoption and improvement
change_network.whatIsIt: A Change Network brings together trusted clinical, operational and admin champions to share clear messages, surface issues early and support peer to peer adoption of $projectName.
change_network.userInsight: Adoption spread through trusted peer to peer influence with champions often emerging organically who helped to drive uptake and sustain engagement over time.
change_network.whyThisMatters:
Building trust enabling two-way engagement helps to drive adoption by involving staff in the change from the start.
 Local networks help to build local confidence and support by using trusted peers.
 Champions can help to surface workflow and template issues early through frontline insight, speeding up improvements.
change_network.quickRealityCheck:
Do you have champions across the right roles, teams and locations? Do network members know what they have been asked to do?
 Has protected time been discussed and agreed with managers? Have feedback channels been set up and shared?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: VISIBLE CHAMPIONS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Champions are visible and active locally with peer learning, coaching and demonstration driving confidence and adoption as part of a Change Network.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: TWO WAY ENGAGEMENT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Two-way engagement is working with clear, consistent messages and early feedback shaping decisions.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: USE OF INSIGHTS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Insights are used to improve rollout, with champions surfacing issues early and informing workflow and template refinement.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: SUPPORTS ADOPTION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The network supports adoption before, during and after launch.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: HELP WITH VALIDATION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Champions help validate real world scenarios and user impacts.

risksIfYouDont.title: LIMITED SUPPORT
risksIfYouDont.body: Limited local support and influence. Change stays centralised with no trusted peers to explain, support and encourage adoption.

risksIfYouDont.title: LOW TRUST
risksIfYouDont.body: Low trust and engagement. People don't feel involved or heard so confidence drops and resistance increases.

risksIfYouDont.title: NO PEER SUPPORT
risksIfYouDont.body: Poor adoption and inconsistent use. Without peer support and reinforcement, take up is patchy and new ways of working don't stick.

risksIfYouDont.title: LACK OF REPRESENTATION
risksIfYouDont.body: Champions are not representative of affected teams.

risksIfYouDont.title: STOPPED ACTIVITY
risksIfYouDont.body: Network activity stops after launch.

benefits.component: What's In It For Me (WIIFM) Benefits
benefits.description: Make the benefits real, relevant and meaningful for everyone
benefits.whatIsIt: What's in it for me (WIIFM) translates $projectName benefits into clear, personal messages so staff can see how the change will make their own work easier or better.
benefits.userInsight: WIIFM benefits landed more effectively when they reflected real practical clinical experience – reduced cognitive load, increased patient focus and clinical safety.
benefits.whyThisMatters:
WIIFM messaging is a primary driver of engagement and can support resistance reduction.
 Role-specific benefits help reduce fear about workforce impact and job loss narratives.
 Credible WIIFM support safer adoption by reinforcing correct use and "Human in the Loop" review and approval of $projectName outputs.
benefits.quickRealityCheck:
Do people understand what's in it for them? Are the benefits relevant to the real workforce pressures?
 Are we communicating WIIFM benefits in the right way? Are people showing they understand the reason for the $projectName introduction?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: STAFF EXPLANATION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Staff can explain the benefits in their own words, not just repeat generic transformation language.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: REAL DAY TO DAY IMPROVEMENTS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Communications focus on real day to day improvements.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CLEAR ADMIN IMPACTS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Admin impacts are clearly explained, including how roles may evolve and how staff will be supported.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: FEEDBACK LED ADOPTION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Concerns are captured and used to refine messaging, training and support.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: ROLE SPECIFIC BENEFITS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Benefits are tailored by audience, especially for clinicians.

risksIfYouDont.title: DOMINATING MYTHS
risksIfYouDont.body: Productivity enforcement myths dominate and reduce uptake.

risksIfYouDont.title: INCREASED ANXIETY
risksIfYouDont.body: Admin staff assume $projectName is workforce reduction leading to increased anxiety.

risksIfYouDont.title: ENTHUSIASM FADES
risksIfYouDont.body: Benefits remain theoretical; enthusiasm fades quickly.

risksIfYouDont.title: TRAINING LANDS POORLY
risksIfYouDont.body: Staff attend training but do not apply $projectName because the 'Why' is unclear.

risksIfYouDont.title: MOMENTUM FADES
risksIfYouDont.body: Early interest drops off before $projectName becomes embedded in ways of working.

stakeholder.description: Engage early and involve staff in shaping how $projectName will work
stakeholder.whatIsIt: Stakeholder Engagement and Communications build understanding, trust and commitment through early, two-way engagement with clinicians, admin teams, leaders and patients.
stakeholder.userInsight: Adoption was strongest where trusted peers led the change, clinical and admin teams were engaged early and patients and clinicians had clarity and confidence around the change.
stakeholder.whyThisMatters:
Engagement reduces resistance by building understanding and addressing misconceptions early.
 When people are involved in design, they become advocates.
 Patient trust and understanding is increased when communication is transparent and choice based.
stakeholder.quickRealityCheck:
Is there a feedback loop after communications go out? Are comms understandable to non-technical staff?
 Are issues tracked through to closure? Are real life scenarios included in validations?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: EARLY INCLUSION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Clinical staff and admin teams are included early in workflow design and feedback loops.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: GOOD PATIENT INFORMATION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Patient information exists in inclusive formats (posters/FAQs) and clinicians can explain it confidently.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: VISIBLE CHAMPIONS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Champions are visible, supported and used as peer-facing demonstrators.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: EARLY ENGAGEMENT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Engagement starts early enough to shape decisions.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: IDENTIFIED STAKEHOLDERS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: All stakeholders are identified by impact, not just seniority

risksIfYouDont.title: RUMOURS AND MISINTERPRETATION
risksIfYouDont.body: Rumour and misinterpretation regarding increased workload and admin replacement, become narratives.

risksIfYouDont.title: FRICTION CAUSES REWORK
risksIfYouDont.body: Workflow issues surface late and create friction and rework.

risksIfYouDont.title: INCREASED PATIENT CONFUSION
risksIfYouDont.body: Patient confusion and uncertainty increases complaints or reduces

risksIfYouDont.title: MISSED RISKS
risksIfYouDont.body: Critical risks or situations where it might struggle in practice (such as complex consultations or noisy environments) are missed.

risksIfYouDont.title: MONITORING CEASE
risksIfYouDont.body: Monitoring stops after it use begins rather than continuing in live use

resistance.description: Understand and address the concerns that could prevent adoption
resistance.whatIsIt: Resistance Management helps organisations identify, understand and address the concerns, perceptions and experiences that may prevent people from adopting a change. It recognises that resistance is often valuable feedback about how a change is being experienced and provides practical approaches to addressing barriers before they affect adoption.
resistance.whyThisMatters:
Resistance can be a natural response to change but often provides important insight into the challenges people are experiencing.
 Many adoption issues are incorrectly labelled as resistance when the underlying cause is unclear communication, poor workflow fit, lack of confidence, insufficient support, competing priorities or previous negative experiences of change.
 Understanding the reasons behind resistance helps organisations address the real issue rather than treating the symptom.
 When concerns are acknowledged and addressed early, organisations can build trust, improve engagement, strengthen adoption and reduce the likelihood of barriers becoming embedded.
resistance.quickRealityCheck:
Do you understand the reasons why people may be reluctant to adopt the change?
 Are concerns being identified and discussed early?
 Can you distinguish between resistance, capability gaps, poor communication and workflow challenges?
 Are leaders, managers and change champions equipped to respond to concerns constructively?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CONCERNS ARE SURFACED EARLY
whatGoodLooksLike.body: People feel able to raise questions, concerns and challenges openly without fear of being labelled negative or resistant.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: THE ROOT CAUSE IS UNDERSTOOD
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The organisation seeks to understand what is driving resistance and addresses the underlying issue rather than making assumptions.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CONCERNS SHAPE CHANGE ACTIONS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Feedback and insight are used to improve communication, engagement, support, leadership activity and implementation approaches.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: LEADERS RESPOND CONSTRUCTIVELY
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Managers, sponsors and change leaders actively listen, address concerns and demonstrate visible action where improvements are needed.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: TRUST IS BUILT THROUGH ACTION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: People see evidence that feedback is taken seriously and results in meaningful improvements, building confidence and credibility.

risksIfYouDont.title: RESISTANCE BECOMES ENTRENCHED
risksIfYouDont.body: Concerns remain unaddressed and gradually become fixed attitudes, behaviours or opposition to the change.

risksIfYouDont.title: THE WRONG PROBLEM IS SOLVED
risksIfYouDont.body: Adoption challenges are treated as resistance when the real issue relates to capability, communication, workflow or support.

risksIfYouDont.title: TRUST DECLINES
risksIfYouDont.body: People become less willing to engage when they feel concerns are ignored, dismissed or misunderstood.

risksIfYouDont.title: WORKAROUNDS EMERGE
risksIfYouDont.body: Individuals and teams develop alternative ways of working to avoid the change rather than adopting the intended approach.

risksIfYouDont.title: ADOPTION STALLS
risksIfYouDont.body: Confidence, engagement and commitment reduce over time, limiting adoption and preventing benefits from being fully realised.

skills_learning.description: Build the capability and confidence needed to adopt new ways of working
skills_learning.whatIsIt: Skills and Learning helps people develop the knowledge, skills and confidence needed to adopt and sustain new ways of working. It focuses on enabling people to apply what they have learned in practice, building capability over time and ensuring support is available when it is needed most.
skills_learning.whyThisMatters:
Digital adoption is not achieved through training alone. People need the confidence, capability and opportunity to apply new knowledge in their day-to-day work.
 Many adoption challenges occur because people understand the change in theory but struggle to apply it in practice. Learning that is disconnected from real workflows, responsibilities and experiences rarely results in sustained adoption.
 Effective learning helps people understand not only how to use a solution, but how their role, behaviours and ways of working may need to change.
 Building capability and confidence reduces uncertainty, increases adoption and helps people adapt successfully as the change becomes part of everyday practice.
skills_learning.quickRealityCheck:
Do people have the knowledge and skills needed to adopt the change successfully?
 Is learning designed around real roles, workflows and day-to-day experiences?
 Can people access support when they need it, not just during formal training?
 Are confidence and capability improving as adoption progresses?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: LEARNING IS RELEVANT TO REAL WORK
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Learning reflects real roles, responsibilities, workflows and scenarios, helping people understand how the change applies to their day-to-day work.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CAPABILITY IS BUILT OVER TIME
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Learning is viewed as an ongoing process, with opportunities to practise, reinforce and develop skills as confidence grows.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: SUPPORT IS AVAILABLE AT THE POINT OF NEED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: People can access guidance, coaching, peer support and resources when they encounter challenges in real situations.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: DIFFERENT NEEDS ARE RECOGNISED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Learning approaches are tailored to different roles, levels of experience, learning preferences and adoption needs.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CONFIDENCE IS ACTIVELY DEVELOPED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Organisations measure and strengthen confidence alongside competence, helping people apply new knowledge successfully in practice.

risksIfYouDont.title: KNOWLEDGE FAILS TO TRANSFER INTO PRACTICE
risksIfYouDont.body: People complete training but struggle to apply what they have learned in their day-to-day work.

risksIfYouDont.title: CONFIDENCE REMAINS LOW
risksIfYouDont.body: Individuals understand what is expected but lack the confidence to change existing behaviours and ways of working.

risksIfYouDont.title: CAPABILITY GAPS REMAIN HIDDEN
risksIfYouDont.body: Critical skills gaps are not identified until they begin to affect performance, adoption or user experience.

risksIfYouDont.title: PEOPLE RELY ON OLD HABITS
risksIfYouDont.body: Individuals revert to familiar processes and behaviours because they feel more confident using existing approaches.

risksIfYouDont.title: ADOPTION PROGRESSES UNEVENLY
risksIfYouDont.body: Some teams develop confidence and capability quickly while others struggle due to inconsistent learning and support.

capability.description: Confidence grows when $projectName makes work easier in practice
capability.whatIsIt: Capability and Confidence focus on building the organisational skills and confidence needed to make $projectName a trusted routine part of everyday practice.
capability.userInsight: Adoption was driven by proven performance in practice through proof of concepts, whilst reliability issues quickly reduced trust.
capability.whyThisMatters:
Capability and confidence determines whether $projectName becomes routine practice or use remains limited.
 Confidence supports safe "Human in the Loop" review and approval of $projectName outputs, even under pressure.
 Internal capability reduces supplier dependence and helps scale up $projectName.
capability.quickRealityCheck:
Can staff use $projectName without step-by-step instructions? Do confidence levels match training completion?
 Have staff had safe practice time? Is peer support available locally?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: RELIABLE $projectName USE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Users can use $projectName reliably in real settings and maintain full clinical responsibility through "Human in the Loop" review and approval.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CHANGE CHAMPIONS SUPPORT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Local champions/super-users exist and are supported with customisation skills.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: IMPROVED COMPLIANCE BEHAVIOURS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Compliance behaviours (e.g. consent recording) improve through reinforcement and clearer workflows.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CONFIDENCE BUILDS GRADUALLY
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Users are supported to move from basic familiarity to confident, routine use.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: LEARNING IS REVISITED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Training is revisited as systems, workflows or staff needs change.

risksIfYouDont.title: STALLED ADOPTION
risksIfYouDont.body: Early trust issues spread socially and adoption stalls.

risksIfYouDont.title: UNSAFE PRACTICES
risksIfYouDont.body: Unsafe practice arises when "Human in the Loop" review and approval and clinical accountability are not embedded.

risksIfYouDont.title: VENDOR DEPENDENCY
risksIfYouDont.body: Organisations remain dependent on vendors for day-to-day optimisation.

risksIfYouDont.title: GENERIC TRAINING
risksIfYouDont.body: Support does not reflect different roles, workflows or confidence levels.

risksIfYouDont.title: LOW CONFIDENCE
risksIfYouDont.body: Some users avoid $projectName because they are uncomfortable with the technology.

change_adoption.description: Focus on how $projectName is used in practice, not just whether it is used
change_adoption.whatIsIt: Change adoption is the extent to which $projectName is used confidently and consistently in day-to-day practice beyond go-live. It involves regularly reviewing real usage and feedback to identify where support or reinforcement is needed.
change_adoption.userInsight: Adoption improved when organisations looked beyond usage data to understand user experience and variation in use, using structured pilots as learning opportunities with clear decision points rather than scaling up too early.
change_adoption.whyThisMatters:
If people don't use $projectName properly, you won't get the benefits and understanding why, helps you fix issues and scale safely.
 Understanding "why not" enables targeted support for low confidence, workarounds and resistance.
 Clear adoption decision points support safe scaling and protects trust.
change_adoption.quickRealityCheck:
Is $projectName being used as intended in real clinical workflows? Is use consistent across different teams and roles?
 Do staff feel confident using $projectName in their day-to-day work? Do you understand why some staff are not using $projectName?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: ACTIVE MONITORING
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Adoption is actively monitored using usage data and feedback from high and low users.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: TARGETED REINFORCEMENT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Targeted support is put in place where needed to support confident and consistent use.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: LEARNING IN PRACTICE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Use early learning to refine support and strengthen stakeholder confidence.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: VISIBLE SUPPORT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Champions are active post go-live providing targeted support to address issues and improve adoption.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CONSISTENT USE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: $projectName is used in a consistent way across teams and services in day-to-day practice.

risksIfYouDont.title: UNREALISED BENEFITS
risksIfYouDont.body: If adoption is inconsistent, the benefits of $projectName will not be realised.

risksIfYouDont.title: PATCHY USE
risksIfYouDont.body: Variation in how $projectName is used across teams leads to inconsistent use, reducing confidence.

risksIfYouDont.title: HIDDEN ISSUES
risksIfYouDont.body: Without understanding why people are not using $projectName, underlying issues are missed.

risksIfYouDont.title: PERSISTENT WORKAROUNDS
risksIfYouDont.body: Low confidence, workarounds and resistance persist without targeted reinforcement, undermining effective use.

risksIfYouDont.title: SCALING TOO EARLY
risksIfYouDont.body: Without clear adoption insights and decision points, organisations risk scaling too quickly.

process_change.description: Make $projectName part of everyday practice – set clear expectations and co-design locally
process_change.whatIsIt: Ways of Working define the new behaviours, habits and expectations needed to use $projectName safely and consistently across different clinical settings.
process_change.userInsight: $projectName only transformed practice when teams changed habits, otherwise old ways persisted.
process_change.whyThisMatters:
Inconsistent practice can emerge across teams and settings.
 Clinicians slip back into old habits rewriting notes or just dictation.
 Safety risks increase when "Human in the Loop" review and approval and clinical ownership drop when it gets busy.
process_change.quickRealityCheck:
Can staff explain how $projectName fits with the workflow? Do supporting materials match actual practice?
 Are workarounds being spotted? Is feedback being used to refine the workflow?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: RECOGNISE GAPS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: As-Is/To-Be workflows are mapped and variations between teams are recognised.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: TAILOR TEMPLATES
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Templates and outputs are deliberately tailored to local workflow requirements.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: RETIRE OLD WORKAROUNDS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Old workarounds are identified and actively retired as the new process stabilises.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: STAFF INVOLVEMENT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Involve the right staff in mapping workflows.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT LOOP
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Feedback from users and operations are used to refine the process

risksIfYouDont.title: WORKAROUNDS BECOME NORMALISED
risksIfYouDont.body: Workarounds become normalised and difficult to reverse.

risksIfYouDont.title: INCONSISTENT PROCESSES
risksIfYouDont.body: Safety and governance risks increase due to inconsistent process routes and identifiers.

risksIfYouDont.title: LOST EFFICIENCY GAINS
risksIfYouDont.body: Efficiency gains are lost due to parallel processes and rework.

risksIfYouDont.title: POOR SCALABILITY
risksIfYouDont.body: It may work in isolated cases but fail at broader rollout.

risksIfYouDont.title: STAKEHOLDER RESISTANCE LATER
risksIfYouDont.body: Adoption becomes harder once expectations and habits are fixed.

reinforcement.description: Sustain adoption by embedding, reinforcing and normalising new ways of working
reinforcement.whatIsIt: Reinforcement helps organisations sustain change by ensuring new behaviours, ways of working and adoption outcomes become part of everyday practice. It focuses on maintaining momentum, addressing barriers, recognising progress and continuously strengthening adoption long after implementation activities have finished.
reinforcement.whyThisMatters:
Implementation introduces change. Reinforcement helps the change last.
 Without reinforcement, people often revert to familiar behaviours, especially when workloads increase, priorities shift or support is reduced. Initial adoption does not automatically translate into sustained adoption.
 Successful digital adoption requires ongoing attention to behaviours, habits, leadership, support and continuous improvement. Reinforcement helps organisations ensure that new ways of working become the normal way of working.
 Effective reinforcement also demonstrates that adoption matters, feedback is valued and improvements continue beyond initial implementation, helping organisations realise and sustain the intended benefits of change.
reinforcement.quickRealityCheck:
Are new behaviours and ways of working being reinforced after implementation?
 Do leaders and managers consistently support and model the change?
 Are feedback, adoption insights and lessons learned being used to drive action?
 Is progress being recognised, celebrated and shared to maintain momentum?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: NEW WAYS OF WORKING BECOME THE NORM
whatGoodLooksLike.body: People consistently apply the expected behaviours, processes and ways of working as part of everyday practice.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: FEEDBACK LEADS TO IMPROVEMENT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Adoption insights, feedback and lessons learned are used to improve support, remove barriers and strengthen adoption.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: LEADERS ACTIVELY REINFORCE CHANGE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Sponsors, managers and leaders continue to champion the change, demonstrate commitment and reinforce expectations through their actions.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: SUCCESS IS VISIBLE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Progress, achievements, improvements and positive outcomes are shared regularly to build confidence and maintain momentum.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: ADOPTION IS CONTINUOUSLY STRENGTHENED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Organisations actively monitor adoption and provide additional support, guidance and intervention where reinforcement is needed.

risksIfYouDont.title: PEOPLE REVERT TO OLD HABITS
risksIfYouDont.body: Individuals and teams gradually return to familiar behaviours because the new ways of working are not actively reinforced.

risksIfYouDont.title: ADOPTION DECLINES OVER TIME
risksIfYouDont.body: Initial enthusiasm reduces and adoption levels fall as attention moves to other priorities and initiatives.

risksIfYouDont.title: FEEDBACK IS IGNORED
risksIfYouDont.body: People stop providing insight and raising issues because they do not see evidence that feedback is being acted upon.

risksIfYouDont.title: BENEFITS FAIL TO BE SUSTAINED
risksIfYouDont.body: Early improvements are achieved but weaken over time because adoption is not maintained and embedded.

risksIfYouDont.title: CHANGE FEELS TEMPORARY
risksIfYouDont.body: People perceive the change as a short-term project rather than a lasting improvement to how work is performed.

org_maturity.description: $projectName success depends on managing adoption, not just implementation.
org_maturity.whatIsIt: Organisational Change Management Maturity helps organisations reflect on their wider ability to manage and sustain change, so change adoption strengthens long-term capability rather than adding to change fatigue.
org_maturity.userInsight: Breaking readiness into clear repeatable categories (leadership, governance, technology, people and service readiness) supported more consistent $projectName success.
org_maturity.whyThisMatters:
Change maturity informs how much support and structure is needed for safe, sustained change.
 It prevents labelling organisations as being resistant, when issues are related to capability, resourcing or readiness gaps.
 It enables repeatable scaling by applying consistent readiness criteria and governance discipline.
org_maturity.quickRealityCheck:
Is $projectName being managed as a people and workflow change? Is there enough change capability?
 Have stakeholders shaped the approach? Are managers and champions equipped?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: STRUCTURED READINESS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Structured readiness criteria are used before scaling.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: USEFUL LEARNING CAPTURED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Learning is captured and reused through evidence and examples.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: REPEATABLE CHANGE PRACTICES
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Change practices become repeatable, with clear ownership, cadence and measures.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: LEADERSHIP ALIGNMENT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Senior leaders are aligned on why $projectName matters and what success look like.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: BENEFITS ARE OWNED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Expected benefits are clearly defined, tracked and owned beyond go live.

risksIfYouDont.title: INCONSISTENT CHANGE
risksIfYouDont.body: Change becomes reactive and inconsistent; fatigue increases as lessons are not implemented.

risksIfYouDont.title: EVIDENCE LED DECISIONS
risksIfYouDont.body: Scaling decisions become enthusiasm driven rather than evidence led.

risksIfYouDont.title: GOVERNANCE GAPS
risksIfYouDont.body: Governance and readiness gaps create avoidable disruption and loss of trust.

risksIfYouDont.title: ADOPTION NOT ACTIVELY MANAGED
risksIfYouDont.body: Focus stays on go live, with limited tracking of usage, confidence or barriers.

risksIfYouDont.title: INSUFFICIENT CHANGE CAPABILITY
risksIfYouDont.body: Teams lack the time, resource or skills to support adoption properly.

transfer_bau.description: Plan how $projectName will be owned and sustained after Go-Live
transfer_bau.whatIsIt: Transfer to BAU ensures $projectName moves from a time-limited rollout into routine clinical and operational practice, with clear ownership, ongoing support and sustained adoption.
transfer_bau.userInsight: Where $projectName remained owned only by a project or digital team, workflow and behaviour issues resurfaced without clear operational accountability.
transfer_bau.whyThisMatters:
Without a clear BAU transition, $projectName risks becoming "something we tried" rather than how we work.
 BAU ownership ensures clinical safety behaviours are maintained under everyday operational pressure.
 Embedding $projectName into BAU enables continuous optimisation (templates, workflows, support) rather than freezing practice at go-live.
transfer_bau.quickRealityCheck:
Can you name who owns $projectName in BAU? Is $projectName being used consistently across teams?
 Do staff know where to go when something goes wrong? Are issues being fixed and improvements made?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CLEAR OWNERSHIP
whatGoodLooksLike.body: There is named BAU ownership for adoption, safety, support and optimisation.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: ACTIVE MONITORING
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Adoption, confidence and safety signals are reviewed.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Feedback loops and reinforcement activity continue after go-live, with visible fixes and updates.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: VISIBLE VALUE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: $projectName performance and benefits are discussed within routine service or operational forums.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: ACCESSIBLE SUPPORT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: People know where to go for support and how to get help quickly.

risksIfYouDont.title: UNCLEAR OWNERSHIP
risksIfYouDont.body: Adoption slowly erodes as early enthusiasm fades and no one "owns" sustained use.

risksIfYouDont.title: REDUCED OVERSIGHT
risksIfYouDont.body: Safety practices (review and approval of $projectName outputs and consent recording) weaken under pressure without reinforcement.

risksIfYouDont.title: PERSISTENT ISSUES
risksIfYouDont.body: Workflow and template issues persist, leading to frustration and workarounds.

risksIfYouDont.title: UNPROVEN VALUE
risksIfYouDont.body: Organisations struggle to evidence value, making further scale or funding decisions harder.

risksIfYouDont.title: LIMITED SUPPORT
risksIfYouDont.body: Support routes are unclear, so issues persist or are ignored.

celebrating_success.description: Seeing successes makes adoption feel real
celebrating_success.whatIsIt: Celebrating successes not only increases morale but it builds support among those that may need to "see it to believe it". Recognition is needed in order to cement or reinforce the change.
celebrating_success.userInsight: Celebrating success was most effective when staff saw what worked from their peers, as real examples from colleagues strengthened engagement and adoption.
celebrating_success.whyThisMatters:
Saying exactly what went well helps everyone feel proud and ready for the next step.
 It creates a culture of appreciation where people feel valued, recognised and encouraged to keep improving.
 It reinforces positive behaviours by showing what good looks like and encouraging others to follow it.
celebrating_success.quickRealityCheck:
Are you celebrating genuine progress, not just activity? Are you recognising small and large successes?
 Do you have a criteria for what success looks like? Are you learning from successes and not just measuring them?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: PROGRESS IS MADE VISIBLE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Achievements are shared clearly so people can see what has improved and why it matters.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: USEFUL LEARNING CAPTURED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Celebrating success includes reflecting on what worked well, so the learning can be used again.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: PEOPLE RECOGNITION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Recognise the people behind the success, including quieter contributions and team effort.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: SUCCESS MEASURES DEFINED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Clear definitions for measuring success is shared and understood.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: TIMELY RECOGNITION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Success is acknowledged soon after it happens, so staff feel their contribution has been noticed and valued.

risksIfYouDont.title: MOTIVATION DROPS
risksIfYouDont.body: People may feel their effort goes unnoticed, which can reduce energy, commitment and enthusiasm.

risksIfYouDont.title: PROGRESS BECOMES INVISIBLE
risksIfYouDont.body: Without celebration, improvements and achievements can be overlooked or forgotten.

risksIfYouDont.title: LEARNING IS LOST
risksIfYouDont.body: If $projectName does not pause to recognise success, it may also miss the opportunity to understand what worked well.

risksIfYouDont.title: CONFIDENCE IS REDUCED
risksIfYouDont.body: Staff may be less likely to take initiative or try new approaches if success is not acknowledged.

risksIfYouDont.title: TEAM SPIRIT WEAKENS
risksIfYouDont.body: A lack of recognition can reduce shared pride, connection and collaboration across $projectName.

risk_management.description: Identify and remove barriers that could prevent successful adoption
risk_management.whatIsIt: Adoption Risks and Barriers focuses on identifying and addressing the factors that could prevent people from adopting, embedding and sustaining new ways of working. It helps organisations understand the human, organisational and behavioural barriers to change so action can be taken before adoption is affected.
risk_management.whyThisMatters:
Digital adoption rarely fails because technology does not work. More often, it fails because the barriers preventing people from changing have not been identified or addressed.

Many of the biggest threats to successful adoption are linked to leadership, stakeholder engagement, competing priorities, confidence, capability, workflow fit and a lack of local ownership rather than technical issues.

Understanding adoption risks early enables organisations to target support, sponsorship, communication and engagement activity where it will have the greatest impact.

Managing adoption risks proactively helps organisations build trust, increase confidence, improve adoption and maximise the likelihood that benefits will be realised and sustained.
risk_management.quickRealityCheck:
Do you understand what could prevent people from adopting this change? 

Have the key barriers to adoption been identified before implementation begins? 

Are leadership, engagement, confidence, capability and workflow risks being actively monitored? 

Could change saturation, competing priorities or multiple initiatives reduce people's ability to engage with this change?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: ADOPTION BARRIERS ARE VISIBLE
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Potential barriers to adoption are identified, discussed openly and regularly reviewed before they begin to affect engagement or implementation.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: PEOPLE RISKS ARE UNDERSTOOD
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The organisation understands where confidence, capability, engagement, ownership or readiness may be low and takes action to address these risks early.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: CHANGE SATURATION IS ACTIVELY MANAGED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The impact of competing priorities, multiple programmes and ongoing organisational change is understood and reflected within implementation plans and adoption activities.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: RISKS DRIVE TARGETED ACTION
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Communication, engagement, sponsorship, learning and support activities are designed to address known barriers rather than applying generic change interventions.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: WARNING SIGNS ARE IDENTIFIED EARLY
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Feedback, stakeholder insight, adoption measures and local intelligence are used to identify emerging risks before they become significant obstacles to adoption.

risksIfYouDont.title: RESISTANCE EMERGES TOO LATE
risksIfYouDont.body: Concerns remain hidden until they become visible through disengagement, avoidance behaviours, low adoption or active opposition.

risksIfYouDont.title: CHANGE SATURATION REDUCES ENGAGEMENT
risksIfYouDont.body: People become overwhelmed by competing demands and multiple initiatives, reducing their ability to engage with and prioritise the change.

risksIfYouDont.title: SUPPORT IS MISDIRECTED
risksIfYouDont.body: Resources are invested in activities that do not address the real barriers preventing adoption.

risksIfYouDont.title: BENEFITS ARE NOT REALISED
risksIfYouDont.body: The solution may be implemented successfully but expected benefits are not achieved because people have not adopted the new ways of working.

risksIfYouDont.title: WORKAROUNDS BECOME NORMALISED
risksIfYouDont.body: Teams develop alternative practices to overcome challenges, leading to inconsistent adoption, reduced confidence and difficulty sustaining the change.

change_impact.description: Understand the human consequences of change before asking people to adopt it
change_impact.whatIsIt: Change Impact helps organisations understand how a change will affect people, roles, responsibilities, behaviours, workflows and ways of working. It provides a structured approach to identifying who is impacted, what will be different and what support is needed to enable successful adoption.
change_impact.whyThisMatters:
Digital adoption is ultimately a human process. People do not adopt technology. They adopt new behaviours, new workflows and new ways of working.

Many adoption challenges occur because organisations focus on implementing the solution without fully understanding the consequences for the people expected to use it. What appears to be resistance is often uncertainty, increased workload, competing priorities, reduced confidence or poorly understood expectations.

Understanding change impact enables organisations to anticipate where adoption challenges may emerge, identify who needs the most support and design interventions that reflect the reality of people's day-to-day experiences.

The better an organisation understands the human consequences of change, the more effectively it can target communication, engagement, sponsorship, learning and support activities to enable successful adoption.
change_impact.quickRealityCheck:
Do you understand how this change will affect different roles, teams and stakeholder groups? 

Can you clearly describe what people will need to start doing, stop doing or do differently? 

Have you identified which groups will experience the greatest level of disruption, uncertainty or behavioural change? 

Are communications, engagement and support activities aligned to the impacts people will actually experience?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: THE HUMAN CONSEQUENCES ARE UNDERSTOOD
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The organisation has a clear understanding of how the change will affect people, roles, responsibilities, relationships, behaviours and day-to-day ways of working.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: HIGH-IMPACT GROUPS ARE IDENTIFIED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The individuals, teams and stakeholder groups most affected by the change are identified early, enabling targeted support and intervention.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: SUPPORT IS ALIGNED TO IMPACT
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Communication, engagement, leadership, learning and adoption activities are tailored according to the level and nature of the impact experienced.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: IMPACT INSIGHTS SHAPE DECISIONS
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Change impact information influences implementation plans, readiness assessments, adoption strategies and prioritisation decisions.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: IMPACTS ARE REVIEWED AS CHANGE EVOLVES
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The organisation continually monitors the effect of the change, identifying emerging impacts and adapting support as adoption progresses.

risksIfYouDont.title: PEOPLE EXPERIENCE SURPRISE CHANGE
risksIfYouDont.body: Individuals are expected to adopt new ways of working without understanding what is changing, why it matters or how it affects them.

risksIfYouDont.title: SUPPORT MISSES THE REAL NEED
risksIfYouDont.body: Generic communication, training and engagement activities are delivered without reflecting the actual challenges people are experiencing.

risksIfYouDont.title: ADOPTION BARRIERS ARE MISUNDERSTOOD
risksIfYouDont.body: Leaders interpret low engagement or resistance as poor attitude rather than recognising the underlying impacts driving those behaviours.

risksIfYouDont.title: UNCERTAINTY AND ANXIETY INCREASE
risksIfYouDont.body: People fill information gaps themselves, leading to assumptions, speculation and reduced confidence in the change.

risksIfYouDont.title: NEW WAYS OF WORKING FAIL TO EMBED
risksIfYouDont.body: The solution is implemented, but expected behaviours and workflows do not become part of everyday practice because the human consequences were never fully understood or addressed.

cm_readiness.description: Create the conditions for adoption before implementation begins
cm_readiness.whatIsIt: Change Management Readiness and Planning helps organisations determine whether the conditions for successful adoption exist and what actions are needed before implementation proceeds. It focuses on understanding whether leaders, managers, teams and stakeholders are prepared, willing and able to adopt the change and identifying the actions needed to strengthen readiness where gaps exist.
cm_readiness.whyThisMatters:
Successful digital adoption depends on more than solution readiness. It depends on people readiness.

Organisations often know whether a system is ready to go live but have less visibility of whether leaders are aligned, managers are prepared, stakeholders are engaged and teams understand what is changing and why.

Readiness and Planning helps organisations identify adoption barriers before implementation begins, reducing the risk of resistance, confusion, poor engagement and delayed benefits realisation.

Understanding readiness enables organisations to focus effort where it is most needed, strengthening leadership, communication, engagement, capability and support before adoption is affected.
cm_readiness.quickRealityCheck:
Do you know whether people are genuinely ready to adopt this change? 

Have leadership, stakeholder, capability and adoption readiness been assessed? 

Do you understand what conditions could help or hinder adoption across different teams or services? 

Are readiness insights shaping implementation decisions, timelines and support activities?

whatGoodLooksLike.title: ADOPTION READINESS IS UNDERSTOOD
whatGoodLooksLike.body: The organisation understands whether leaders, managers, teams and stakeholders are prepared to adopt and support the change.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: READINESS GAPS ARE IDENTIFIED EARLY
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Potential barriers relating to leadership, engagement, capability, ownership or support are identified before implementation begins.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: PLANS REFLECT ADOPTION REALITY
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Implementation plans are informed by readiness insights and recognise that different teams and stakeholder groups may require different levels of support.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: READINESS DRIVES DECISION MAKING
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Readiness findings influence priorities, sequencing, implementation decisions and adoption activities rather than being treated as a compliance exercise.

whatGoodLooksLike.title: READINESS IS CONTINUOUSLY REVIEWED
whatGoodLooksLike.body: Readiness is reassessed throughout the change lifecycle so emerging issues, changing circumstances and adoption risks can be identified and addressed.

risksIfYouDont.title: IMPLEMENTATION OUTPACES ADOPTION
risksIfYouDont.body: The solution is introduced before people are ready, creating avoidable confusion, uncertainty and low adoption.

risksIfYouDont.title: READINESS GAPS REMAIN HIDDEN
risksIfYouDont.body: Issues relating to leadership, engagement, ownership, capability or support are not recognised until implementation is already underway.

risksIfYouDont.title: SUPPORT ARRIVES TOO LATE
risksIfYouDont.body: Organisations only discover adoption challenges after confidence has reduced and negative perceptions have become established.

risksIfYouDont.title: CHANGE SATURATION IS OVERLOOKED
risksIfYouDont.body: Competing priorities and multiple changes reduce people's capacity to engage, but the impact is not recognised or addressed within plans.

risksIfYouDont.title: BENEFITS ARE DELAYED OR LOST
risksIfYouDont.body: Expected outcomes take longer to achieve because the conditions required for successful adoption were not established before implementation began.
